caseno: Criminal Misc. Case No. 24 of 1984, and Sao Motu Rule No. 41 of 1984
lawyer:
Sultan Ahnzad, D. A. G. with Quazi Akhter Hossain A. A. G., Md. Anser Ali and. Md. Altafur Ralmran.— For the State. 

Azizul Hoque and S. M. Amin Azhar—ror the Petitioner (Opposite-parties).
parties:
The State ------ Appellant
Vs.
Abdul Karim Sarkar------ Respondent
full_judgment:
In Criminal Misc. Case No. 24 of 1984 the contemner Mr. Abdul Karim Sarker, Upazilla Nirbahi Officer (U.N.O), Chilmari, District Kurigram was asked to show cause on 19.3.84 why he shall not be convicted for contempt of Court for interfering with the administration of the justice by putting various pressures on Mr. A.K.M. Zulfiquer Ali, Munsif-Magistrate, Chilmari Upazilla, Kurigram. The Rule was issued on the basis of the following facts which were brought to the notice of this Court on a reference made by the learned District and Sessions Judge, Rangpur upon a complaint dated 28.12.83 lodged by the said Munsif-Magistrate:— 

 1. That on 6-12.83 while the said Munsif-Magistrate was conducting criminal cases sitting in Court the U.N.O. Abdul Karim Sarker, Chilmari Upzilla, Kurigram sat by his Gide and uttered in presence of Advocates, Court sub-inspector and litigants present that the said Munsif-Magistrate should get practical training from him as to how cases are filed, how depositions are written, under what section depositions are recorded and matters like these. 

 2. That on 26-12-83 the said U.N.O. summoned the said Munsif-Magistrate in his chamber in respect of a pending case in presence of one of the parties to a criminal proceeding and directed the Munsif-Magistrate to dispose of the case according to his instructions and advice. Further from 27-12-83 the said U.N.O. instructed the Bench Officer of the Criminal Court and others not to work in the Court of the Munsif-Magistrate and thereby the normal judicial works of the Court suffered. 

 3. This Court on perusal of the two representations issued a suo motu Rule of contempt on 30-4-84 asking the aforesaid U.N.O. to show cause why he shall not be punished for repeating the offence of contempt of Court. It has been alleged in the said representations that the safety and security of the life of the Munsif-Magistrate was at stake as the U.N.O. had set up people to assault him after issuance of the first contempt Rule. The second contempt Rule has been numbered as Criminal Misc. Case No. 41 of 1984. 

 1. An affidavit by the contemner sworn and filed on 18-4-84 in Criminal Misc. Case No. 24 of 1984. We shall call it the first affidavit. 

 2. Further affidavit by the contemner sworn and filed on 29.5-84 in Criminal Misc, Case No. 41 of 1984. We shall call it the 2nd affidavit. 

 3. An affidavit-in-reply sworn and filed by the Munsif-Magistrate on 10-7-84 in Criminal Misc. Case No. 24 of 1984. We shall call it the 3rd affidavit. 4. Further affidavit by the contemner in Criminal Misc. Case No. 24 of 1984 sworn and filed on 20-8-84. We shall call it the 4th affidavit. 

 5. Further affidavit by the Munsif-Magistrate in Criminal Misc. Case No. 24 of 1984 sworn and filed on 15-11-84. We shall call it the 5th affidavit. 

 6. Further affidavit by the Munsif-Magistrate in Criminal Misc. Case No. 41 of 1984 sworn and filed on 15-11-84. We shall call it the 6th affidavit. 

 7. An affidavit-in-reply by the contemner in Criminal Misc. Case No. 24 of 1984 sworn and fled on 25-11-84. We shall call it the 7th affidavit. 

 8. An affidavit-in-reply by the contemner in Misc. Case No. 41 of 1984 sworn and filed on 25-11-84. We shall call it the 8th affidavit. The main defence of the contemner with regard to the allegations in Criminal Misc. Case No. 24 of 1984 is contained in the first affidavit. 

 6. The contemner received from the Munsif-Magistrate an information on 27-11-83 that the Munsif-Magistrate was invested with first class power on 10-11-83. The Munsif-Magistrate came to the office-cum-residence of the contemner one day and requested him to "show" the procedure for taking cognizance of cases and other related matters in presence of Mr. Khagendra Nath Barman, Upazilla Education Officer and Mr. Abdur Rashid Sarker, Upazilla Rural Development officer. The contemner told the Munsif-Magistrate that it was too early for him to know about the procedure as he was still not invested with the powers under section 190(1) (a) and (b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Section 190(1) (a) & (b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides inter alia that any Magistrate specially empowered in this behalf may take cognizance of any offence (a) upon receiving in writing of such facts which constitute the offence; (b) upon report in writing of such facts made by any police officer. The Munsif-Magistrate replied that there was no harm in learning the procedure beforehand, as the power would be coming in due course. He received the power subsequently on 29-1-84. On 6-12-83 before going to Court to deal with police and general file the contemner learnt that the Munsif-Magiatrate was holding his, criminal file. The contemner sent Mr. Solaiman Ali, Office Assistant, to enquire of the Munsif-Magistrate if he had time to sit with the contemner to observe the procedure of holding general and police file. Mr. Solaiman Ali reported that the Munsif-Magistrate had finished his criminal cases and was agreeable to sit with hint The contemner wont to court too bold polio, and general file and he sat by the side of the Munsif-Magistrate and started taking police and general file. The Munsif-Magistrate eagerly observed the procedure and also asked him some relevant questions to which the contemner replied and the matter ended there. The contemner denies that he uttered in presence of Advocates, Court Sub-inspector and the litigants present that the Munsif-Magistrate should get practical training from him as to how cases were filed, how depositions were recorded, under what section the depositions were recorded and matters like these. 

 8. With regard to the allegations that the contemner summoned the Munsif-Magistrate on 26-12-83 in his chamber in respect of a pending case in presence of one of the parties to a criminal proceeding and that he directed him to dispose of the case according to his instructions and advice, the contemner denied the same as wholly incorrect and stated that the allegation was totally vague as the case number, names of the parties and other matters related thereto had not been stated. 

 9. With regard to the further allegation that the contemner interfered with the normal judicial works of the Munsif-Magistrate by instructing the Bench Officer of the criminal Court and others not to work in the Court of the Munsif-Magistrate, the contemner denied the same and stated that this would be evident from the criminal case record of the Munsif-Magistrate. The contemner had some discussion with the Munsif-Magistrate regarding the engagement of the Civil Court Peshker as a Bench clerk in criminal cases as well during the leave or absence of the regular Criminal Court Peshker but the Munsif-Magistrate opined that the Civil Court Peshker having had no training in criminal matters would be unable to act as a Bench clerk in criminal cases. The matter ended there and the contemner never instructed the Criminal Court Peshker not to work in the Court of the Munsif-Magistrate. The contemner also denied that he asked Rajkumar, sweeper of the court not to clean the court of the Munsif-Magistrate. Annexure 'F' to the first affidavit contains a statement by Rajkumar dated 4-2-84 to the effect that the Munsif-Magistrate obtained his signature on a piece of paper forcibly. Annexure 'F' was also ad-dressed to the U.N.O. 

 9A. With regard to the allegations that the contemner interfered with the leave and annual vacation of the Munsif-Magistrate, the contemner denied the same and stated that he was directed by the Deputy Commissioner, Rangpur on 18-8-83 as per decision of the Zonal Martial Law Administrator, Zone-B dated 14-8-83 to ask Certificate Officers to issue 24 hours notice to the defaulter loanees to clear up the loans and issue distress warrant thereafter. The Munsif-Magistrate was vested with certificate powers by the Divisional Commissioner, Rajshahi. The contemner simply informed the Deputy Commissioner, Rangpur by memo No. 32-C dated 6-10-83 of the fact that as the Munsif-Magistrate was on leave due to Civil Court vacation from 2-10-83 it was not possible to dispose of those cases. The said memo dated 6-10-83 was annexed as Annexure 'I' to the first affidavit. Annexure 'J' is the decision of the Zonal Martial Law Administrator Zone-B dated 14-8-83. 

 11. We wish to make it clear that the first affidavit is not an affidavit begging unconditional apology from the Court. It is an affidavit contesting and challenging the rule and seeking to establish an alternative case. The apology which has been tendered at the end is not an apology at all. There is absolutely no acknowledgement whatsoever that the contemner committed any contempt of court. He has emphatically challenged the facts stated in the contempt Rule and he does not himself concede that his conduct amounts to Contempt of Court. He leaves it to the court to decide whether he has committed any contempt of Court at all and if the Court so finds then he advances an apology. If the contemner is found guilty of contempt of Court, then such defence aggravates the contempt. 

 12. In his second affidavit the contemner stated that he was absent from Chilmari on official duties from 29-3-84 to 1-4-84 till about 8 P.M. He received the notice of the Contempt Rule in Criminal Misc. Case No. 24 of 1984 on 2-4-84. It is, therefore, absurd that he hatch a conspiracy against the Munsif-Magistrate after issuance of the Contempt Rule to assault him. The allegations of the Munsif-Magistrate were enquired into by the Additional Superintendent of Police, Kurigram on 10-4-84 and by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (General), Kurigram on 15-4-84 and both of them found the same to be baseless and motivated. The contemner annexed the enquiry reports of the said two officers as Annexures 'C' and 'D' respectively to the 2nd affidavit. 

 14. The Munsif-Magistrate also challenged Annexures 'B'-'G' and Annexure 'K' to the first affidavit as concocted, fabricated, manufactured and ante-dated documents created for the purpose of the Contempt Rule with the help of the sycophants and henchmen of the contemner and denied the contents thereof. He contends that the contemner never referred any matter regarding his conduct to his higher authority. The U.N.O. was not in any way his superior officer and as such the U.N.O. was absolutely incompetent to enquire into any matter connected with his conduct. He also stated that on 6-12-83 the contemner started lecturing the Munsif-Magistrate in his Court room while he was holding trial of a criminal case in presence of Mr. Nurul Islam, Advocate, Mr. Nurul Haque or Huda, G.R.O. and C.S.-in-charge, Mr. Abdul Awal, Bench Clerk (Criminal), Naba Kumar Mahanto, Court police, Abul Kalam Azad. Process Server and the litigant public with intent to annoy insult and humiliate him. He reiterated his earlier statements made in his memo dated 28.12.83 addressed to the learned District & Sessions Judge, Rangpur. 

 15. The Munsif-Magistrate disclosed in the 3rd affidavit that the contemner asked him to dispose of a pending criminal case, namely, G.R. Case No. 18 of 1983 Chilmari according to his instructions and advice. He also annexed Annexure 5, a written statement by Md. Awal Mia, Bench Clerk, Chilmari Magistrate's Court stating that he was instructed by the contemner not to work in the Court of the Munsif-Magistrate. He also enclosed various complaints & representations made in connection with the contemner's making his life miserable at Chilmari. He further stated that for his safety and security he has been transferred from Chilmari but the contemner- U.N.O. was still serving as U.N.O. Chilmari until be is transferred from Chilmari the Munsif-Magistrate will not be able to procure witnesses to prove his case. In the 4th affidavit the contemner repudiated the contentions of the Munsif-Magistrate in the 3rd affidavit. 

 21. Now, his defence is that the Munsif-Magistrate wanted to learn from him in advance how to take cognizance of cases under section 190(1) (a) and (b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and accordingly he showed him the procedure on 6-12-83 with his consent. 

 22. Mr. Sultan Ahmed learned Deputy Attorney General who was asked by the Court to appear in the Rules for the prosecution of the contemner, has produced before us Notification No. JAIV/19/83-954 dated 10-11-83 and Notification No. JAIV/19/83-956 dated 10-11-83, both issued by the Ministry of Establishment and Re-organisation of the Government of Bangladesh. The first Notification vests the Munsif-Magistrate Mr. K.M. Zulfiquer Ali, Chilmarl, Rangpur (now Kurigram) with the powers of a Magistrate of the 1st class to try criminal cases within the jurisdiction of his Upazilla. The contemner admits that he was aware of the first Notification on 27.11.83, i.e. before 6.12.83. The second Notification vests him with the powers under section 190 (1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Both Notifications are dated 10.11.83. Section 190(1)(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides inter-alia that any Magistrate specially empowered in this behalf may take cognizance of any offence upon information received from any person other than a Police Officer or upon his own knowledge or suspicion. 

 23. Therefore, the Munsif-Magistrate in the instant case was empowered as early as on 10.11.83 to try criminal cases as a first class Magistrate and to take cognizance of any offence upon complaint or suo motu. When he had such powers it will be presumed -that he was given necessary training to exercise these powers. It in an absur4 and preposterous proposition that he will want to know from the U.N.O. as to how cases are filed, depositions are recorded and under what section depositions are recorded when he already knows how criminal cases are tried and how cognizance is taken upon complaint or suo motu. We are, therefore, convinced that no occasion arose obliging the Munsif-Magistrate to sit with the contemner to observe how he disposed of general and police file. Once a Magistrate knows how to take cognizance of cases u/s. 190(1)(c) Cr.P.C., he also knows how to do the same u/s. 190(1)(a) & (b) Cr.P.C. The contemner has put up an unworthy and unbelievable defence and we have no manner of doubt that he has concocted a cock and bull story to hide his guilt. 

 25. We are simply amazed to find that the contemner should have at all put up such a flimsy and easily detectable invalid excuse. The contemner should know that the office of the U.N.O. is a recent phenomenon, but the office of the Munsif is about two centuries old. The people of our country, whether literate or illiterate, more so a member of a Union Parishad, exactly knows to whom a complaint should be addressed when the conduct of a Munsif is involved. He knows that a Munsif's conduct can be enquired into only by his superior officer, namely, the learned District and Sessions Judge. A man of ordinary prudence in our country will never address a communication to the U.N.O. against the judicial or extra-judicial conduct of a Munsif. Therefore, on the face of it Annexure, 'B', a complaint by a member of a Union Parishad, is a manufactured document created for the purpose of this Rule and we do not place any reliance on the same. Annexures 'C', 'B' and 'K' are complaints lodged by various Upazilla level officers to the U.N.O. against the conduct of the Munsif-Magistrate. It is indeed very strange that all these complaints allegedly started pouring into the office of the U.N.O. after the incident on 6-12-83. These Upazilla level officers, as we have seen in the Resolution of the Government, have all been placed directly under the contemner U.N.O. Be writes their Annual Confidential Reports, Like the contemner these Upazilla level officers have also con-veniently forgotten that the Munsif-Magistrate is not accountable to the U.N.O. for his conduct. Common sense, propriety, decency, discipline and Government Rules and Resolutions have been given a go by and those Upazilla level officers have poured scorn on the Munsif-Magistrate in written complaints with the U.N.O. The contemner U.N.O. in his turn had the insolence and impudence not only to entertain those complaints but also to take some actions in the matter. He asked his subordinate Upazilla level officers to report on the matter instead of forwarding the complaints to the learned District and Sessions Judge. Those Upazilla level officers also merrily enquired into the conduct of the Munsif-Magistrate and submitted a report Annexure 'D' to the U.N.O. It is one of those officers whom the contemner wants to examine as a witness in these Rules. We shudder to think at what low level the mentality of these junior officers had sunk. These activities on the part of the Upazilla level officers and the contemner U.N.O. are by themselves contemptuous of the person and honour of the Munsif Magistrate. We have no hesitation in finding that. Annexures B,C,D,E,F and K to the first affidavit are concocted, got-up and manufactured documents created for the purpose of these Rules. The contemner has set up a palpably false and frivolous case to purge himself of the offence of contempt of Court. 

 26. We are, therefore, not prima fade satisfied about the bonafides of the contemner's defence. His alternative version has no basis at all. It is purely a smokescreen designed to create a cloud and a smoke. The question of examining witnesses does not arise at all. The witnesses that the contemner wants to examine are very much under his thumb. They are his direct subordinates or persons on whom he wields immense influence by virtue of his continuing position as the Chief Executive of the Upazilla. We do not think that in the facts and circumstances of this case examination of witnesses is at all warranted. On the face of it the contemner has put up a false and fabricated defence. 

 27. The incident of sitting by the side of the Munsif-Magistrate and telling him in presence of Advocates and litigants as to how to conduct a criminal case is an unprecedented and unwarranted interference with the administration of justice. It is deliberately calculated to lower the image of judiciary in public eyes. It is a contumacious disregard of the dignity of a Court of law which must be visited with appropriate punishment. We find the contemner guilty of contempt of Court on this allegation. 

 28. With regard to the allegation that the Munsif-Magistrate was asked to dispose of a particular case according to the instructions and advice of the contemner U.N.O. we find that the allegation was vague. It was only in the reply that the Munsif-Magistrate annexed the particulars. In that view of the matter we do not think that the contemner can be held guilty of Contempt of Court on that account and we absorbed him of this allegation. But with regard to the allegation that the contemner instructed the Bench Officer of the Criminal Court and others not to work in the Court of the Munsif-Magistrate, we are satisfied with the statement of the Bench Officer, Vide Annexure '5' to the 3rd affidavit to the effect that the contemner U.N.O. did ask him not to work in the Court of the Munsif-Magistrate. This is a gross interference with the working of the Court and we find the contemner guilty of contempt of Court on this allegation as well. We are not taking into account the statement of Rajkumar, the sweeper as the contempt Rule did not specifically draw the attention of the contemner in the matter. 

 32. As for the Rule in Criminal Misc. Case No. 41 of 1984, we do not think that the apprehension of the Munsif-Magistrate that the contemner U.N.O. was organising hooliguns to assault him after issuance of the Rule in Criminal Misc. Case No. 24 of 1984 has been substantiated by any cogent evidence or circumstance on record. It remains only an apprehension and no conviction can be based on a mere apprehension. 

 34. The contemner has behaved in the most reprehensible manner possible. He has twisted the arms of the Munsif-Magistrate in the crudest form. His defence in the contempt Rule is all the more reprehensible. He has no regrets, no remorse. He has chosen to defend his actions with fabricate papers and documents. His conduct can only cause despair and dismay. He deserves no consideration whatsoever in so far as sentence is concerned. 35. In the result, the Rule in Criminal Misc. Case No. 24 of 1984 is made absolute. The contemner Abdul Karim Sarker, U.N.O. (Upazilla Nirbahi Officer), Chilmari, District Kurigram is found guilty of gross contempt of Court and is convicted of the same. He is sentenced to suffer simple imprisonment for 7 (seven) days and to pay a fine of Tk.1000/- in default, to suffer simple imprisonment for ; days Lots, The Rule in Criminal Misc. Case No. 41 of 1984 is discharged. The contemner is found not guilty of the allegations made in the said Rule. Let a copy of this judgment be transmitted to the Secretary, Cabinet Division, Secretary, Establishment Division and Secretary, Ministry of Law for information. Let a copy each of Notification Nos. JAIV/- 19/83-954 and 956 both dated 10.11. 83 be kept with the record duly attested by the learned Deputy Attorney General.
